en: The Sūtra on Being Drifted by Water-Bubbles, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the Palace of Ajātaśatru, which King Prasenajit had built, on the banks of the Ganges River.
To one side, he was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a large mass of foam being carried away by the water.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this mass of foam being carried away by the Ganges River? The bhikṣus replied, "We do."
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:

"Regarding this mass of foam, if a person with sight were to observe it closely, contemplate it, and analyze it—having seen it, observing it closely, contemplating it, and analyzing it—they would find it empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity."
"What reliance can there be upon this mass of froth?
In the same way, whatever forms there are—past, future, or present; whether gross or subtle; whether far or near—a person with sight should observe them closely, contemplate them, and discern them."

Having seen this, that person examines it closely and reflects upon it with discernment: it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going; being empty and non-existent, it is also not solid. What solidity is there in this aggregate of form?
It is like the appearance of bubbles in summer rain: some arise and some perish; a person with sight observes them closely and reflects upon them with discernment.

That person, having seen the truth and observed it through contemplation and discernment, perceives that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity; just as with this water-froth, what solidity could there be?

In this way, regarding the pains within this body—whether of the future, past, or present; whether coarse or subtle; whether pleasant or unpleasant; whether distant or near—a person with eyes observes them clearly, contemplates them, and analyzes them.

Having already observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, he realizes that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and not solid; what solidity is there within this aggregate of sensation?

It is, for example, like the midday sun in the summer months when there are no clouds to obscure it; the shimmering heat rises intensely, and a man with sight observes it, contemplates it, and analyzes it.
Having thus observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, he realizes that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity; for what solidity can there be in this mirage?

In this way, whatever perceptions there may be—whether past, future, or present; whether coarse or subtle; whether beautiful or ugly; whether distant or near—a person with vision observes them, contemplates them, and analyzes them.

Having already observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, he sees that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity; what solidity is there within this aggregate of perception?

It is, for example, like a person who leaves a city or village seeking a solid vessel and goes into a great thicket of trees. If they see a plantain tree growing lush and beautiful, which delights those who behold it, yet stands alone without branches or leaves; and if they cut its root into three or four pieces and strip away the layers of bark wherever they find them, they cannot find any core within, much less anything solid.
A person with eyes observes it closely, contemplates it, and analyzes it.

Having observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, they see that it is empty and devoid of anything real, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity. What solidity can there be in this plantain tree?

In this way, whatever formations there are—whether past, future, or present; whether gross or subtle; whether excellent or inferior; whether distant or near—a person with eyes observes them, contemplates them, and discerns them.

Having already observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, one realizes that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and not solid; in this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), what solidity can there be?

It is like a clever illusionist or an illusionist’s apprentice who, before a great multitude, manifests his own illusory arts; if there were a person with clear vision who observed them closely, contemplated them, and analyzed them.
Having already observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, he sees that it is empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and not solid; how could this magical illusion possess any solidity?

In this way, whatever consciousnesses there may be—whether past, future, or present; whether coarse or subtle; whether beautiful or ugly; whether distant or near—a person with eyes observes them closely, contemplates them, and discerns them.

Having already observed, contemplated, and analyzed it, he finds it to be empty and non-existent, neither coming nor going, and lacking any solidity; what solidity, then, can there be in this aggregate of consciousness?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Form is like a mass of foam; Sensation is like a bubble on the water;
Perception is like a summer mirage; Volitional formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree."
Consciousness is like that magical illusion, as taught by the Most Victorious One.
If one can observe it with precision, contemplating and discerning it,
even emptiness will be found to have no existence.
Examine this body as taught by the one of great wisdom:
these three factors must be extinguished, and one must abandon and remove form;
this practice is likewise like the unreal arts of a magician.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on Being Driven by Water Froth, as Spoken by the Buddha.
